strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: adapting web agents to new environments without human-annotated tasks/trajectories or test-set leakage, which is a genuine pain point in current web-agent literature.

The dual-refinement design (task refinement during trajectory collection + post-hoc trajectory refinement) is a sensible, clearly articulated extension of prior work (OS-Genesis, Explorer), and the paper does a good job explaining conceptually why underspecified initial tasks lead to noisy trajectories.

Reasonably thorough empirical protocol: consistent LLM (GPT-4.1) across all baselines and the proposed method for fair comparison, two different open-source backbone models (Qwen2.5-VL-7B, UI-TARS-1.5-7B), and a controlled, reproducible environment (WebArena with Docker) rather than a live website.

Multiple complementary analyses beyond headline accuracy: task diversity via t-SNE and quality scores, trajectory completion-rate breakdown (completed/failed/exceeded budget), API cost comparison, component-wise ablation (SS/CE/TR/JR), and data-scaling curves.
Illustrative case studies (Figures 5–6) make the refinement mechanism concrete and interpretable, aiding understanding of what the method actually does.
weaknesses: All data-quality and diversity metrics (Tables 2–3, t-SNE distances) are produced by GPT-4.1-as-judge, the very same model used to generate and refine the synthetic data. This creates a circularity/self-preference risk: the model may rate its own outputs and refinement style favorably, undermining the claimed "quality" gains as independent evidence; no human verification of task feasibility or trajectory correctness is reported.

Absolute success rates are low and, more importantly, internally inconsistent with the paper's own framing: SynthAgent's synthetic-data model (e.g., 20.80% for Qwen) sometimes exceeds the stated "upper bound" SFT model trained on real test-set tasks (16.37%), which is not adequately explained and calls into question either the upper-bound framing, evaluation protocol, or comparability of training set sizes/qualities.

Evaluation uses a reduced WebArena set (226/812 tasks, one per template) with small per-site counts (26–57), and no repeated runs, variance, or confidence intervals are reported for any table, making it hard to judge whether the reported gains (e.g., +5.1 avg over OS-Genesis) are statistically meaningful rather than noise, especially given per-site results are quite volatile (e.g., UI-TARS Shopping: Ours ties OS-Genesis at 20.00 vs 21.82).

The Explorer baseline's very poor, near-degenerate performance (4.44%/4.96%, 68.3% of trajectories exceeding budget) is surprising given it is a published, peer-reviewed method; since it was re-implemented by the authors rather than using original code/checkpoints, there is a risk the reimplementation disadvantages this comparator, which is central to the paper's contrastive narrative.

Method contribution is somewhat incremental — it is essentially the combination of ideas from OS-Genesis (categorized/triplet-based exploration) and Explorer (iterative task refinement) plus a new post-hoc trajectory-cleaning step, with limited theoretical grounding for the specific heuristics (the hallucination predicate C, the four conservative edit types) beyond intuitive design choices.

Reproducibility is only partially supported: code is promised ("will be publicly available") but not provided at submission, and reliance on a closed proprietary API (GPT-4.1) for all synthesis/refinement/judging steps limits exact reproducibility and independent verification by other researchers.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically relevant problem: adapting web agents to new environments via fully synthetic supervision, with a clear articulation of the specific failure modes (task hallucination, trajectory noise) that motivate the method.

The dual-refinement design (task refinement during collection + post-hoc trajectory refinement) is a sensible and clearly explained combination of ideas, and the paper provides a systematic ablation (Table 4) that isolates the contribution of categorized exploration, task refinement, and trajectory refinement, showing each component matters and that trajectory refinement is necessary to realize the benefit of task refinement.

Comparisons against multiple relevant and reasonably strong baselines (Self-Instruct, OS-Genesis, Explorer) across two different open-source backbone agents (Qwen2.5-VL, UI-TARS) and five WebArena websites give a fairly comprehensive empirical picture.

Additional diagnostic analyses (t-SNE task diversity, trajectory completion/exceed rates, cost comparison, data scaling curve) go beyond simple end-task accuracy and help explain why SynthAgent outperforms Explorer/OS-Genesis (e.g., Explorer's frequent goal changes lead to 68.3% of trajectories exceeding the step budget).

Use of WebArena (Dockerized, controllable) supports reproducibility of the evaluation environment, and the appendix provides full prompts for every refinement/generation stage, aiding replication of the pipeline.
weaknesses: Nearly all fine-grained quality metrics (task quality, task diversity, trajectory quality/completion rates in Tables 2-3) are scored by GPT-4.1, the same model used for task/trajectory generation and refinement in SynthAgent. This creates a circularity/self-evaluation bias that is not discussed or mitigated (e.g., via a second independent judge model or human validation), weakening confidence in these auxiliary claims even though the downstream fine-tuning results offer a more independent check.

Absolute downstream performance remains low and leaves a substantial gap to the SFT (test-task) upper bound, particularly for UI-TARS (17.26% vs 23.45%), and even the fine-tuned models often underperform zero-shot GPT-4.1 (25.22%). This tempers the practical impact of the proposed adaptation despite the relative gains over other synthetic baselines.

The evaluation set is small (226 tasks total, e.g., only 26 for Reddit), and no variance/significance analysis (multiple seeds, confidence intervals) is reported, making it hard to assess whether the reported gains (often a few points) are statistically robust, especially given some tied/coincidental values across methods (e.g., identical Shopping scores for +Self-Instruct/+Ours on UI-TARS).

The Explorer baseline underperforms even the un-adapted base model by a wide margin, which is explained qualitatively (authentication issues, frequent task drift) but not otherwise validated; since this is a reimplementation with different backbone LLM (GPT-4.1) than the original paper, there is a risk that baseline underperformance is partly an artifact of reimplementation choices rather than intrinsic to the method, and no sanity check against reported Explorer numbers is provided.

Evaluation is confined to a single benchmark family (WebArena's five fixed simulated websites), so claims about "adapting to new environments" are not tested on genuinely diverse or real-world websites; external validity beyond this controlled testbed is unverified.

Several implementation choices (context window of 3, up to 2 sampled elements per category, 500 task-trajectory pairs per site) are stated as empirically set without ablation, leaving their sensitivity/robustness unexamined.

The framing of "without human involvement" slightly overstates the contribution, since the method depends on carefully hand-engineered refinement predicates (ExistsUI, MissingArgs, Stall) and multiple detailed prompts crafted by the authors; the novelty is more in combining/refining existing synthetic-data ideas than introducing fundamentally new techniques.

strengths: Clearly identifies and motivates two concrete failure modes in prior synthetic web-agent data pipelines (task hallucination and trajectory noise), framing them as a coherent design tension between environment grounding and execution noise.

The proposed dual refinement (conflict-triggered task refinement during execution + post-hoc global trajectory refinement) and categorized exploration are sensible, well-motivated design choices, and the paper provides detailed qualitative case studies (Figures 5-6) illustrating how each component behaves.

Reasonably broad empirical evaluation: results on both a controlled benchmark (WebArena, 5 websites) and a more realistic large-scale benchmark (Online-Mind2Web, 136 websites), with two different open-source backbone agents (Qwen2.5-VL-7B, UI-TARS-1.5-7B).
Thorough ablations (categorized exploration, task refinement, trajectory refinement) and a data-scaling study that support the claimed contribution of each component.

Quality/diversity metrics are cross-validated with three different LLM judges (GPT-4.1, GPT-5.1, Qwen3-30B), showing consistent relative rankings across baselines, which somewhat strengthens confidence in the comparative claims.
Detailed appendix with prompts, implementation details, and statistics that aid reproducibility of the pipeline (though full code release is not verifiable from the manuscript).
weaknesses: A central soundness concern: the paper frames SFT-on-test-tasks as an 'upper bound,' yet for the Qwen backbone SynthAgent (20.80 overall) actually outperforms this supposed upper bound (16.37), which is not adequately explained and raises questions about the reliability/comparability of the main WebArena results.

Evaluation set for WebArena is small (226 tasks, one run per condition apparently), and no variance, multiple seeds, or significance testing is reported anywhere in the paper, making it hard to assess whether the reported gains (e.g., +5.1 over OS-Genesis) are robust to noise inherent in LLM-based generation/evaluation and stochastic agent rollouts.

Quality/diversity metrics rely entirely on LLM-as-judge scoring, and the same GPT-4.1 model used to synthesize/refine SynthAgent's data is also used as one of the primary judges, creating potential circularity that could bias quality/diversity comparisons in the method's favor; no human evaluation is included to validate these automatic scores.

The Explorer baseline's very poor performance (near-zero success rate on several websites, 68.3% budget overruns) seems disproportionately weak relative to its reported performance in its original paper; while the authors attempt to justify this via re-implementation details, the magnitude of degradation (sometimes below the untrained base model) raises concern about whether the re-implementation is fully faithful/fair, which is important since Explorer is one of the two main points of comparison.

The diversity metric (a single scalar score per method, with t-SNE visualization) is only loosely described, without clear methodology for how the numeric diversity score is computed from embeddings, limiting reproducibility of this specific analysis.
Absolute success rates remain low across the board (roughly 15-30%), and the practical significance/impact of the reported gains for real-world deployment is not deeply discussed.

The code repository link is not filled in in the abstract, and while this may be for anonymity, it leaves reproducibility of the full pipeline (which involves many LLM-prompted stages) unverifiable at review time.
